summary: Binary, denary and hexadecimal number systems, converting between them, why hexadecimal is used, and binary addition and multiplication.

blocks.content: A **number system** is defined by its **base** — how many different digits it uses. The value of a digit depends on its **place value**, a power of the base.

blocks.title: Why computers use binary
blocks.content: Computer circuits are made of transistors that have **two states** — on/off (1/0). Two states are easy to make reliable, so all data and instructions are stored as binary digits (**bits**). 8 bits = 1 **byte**; 4 bits = 1 **nibble**.

blocks.text: Binary → denary: add the place values of the 1s

blocks.title: Method 1 — subtract place values (91)
items: Largest place value ≤ 91 is 64 → bit 1, remainder 27.

blocks.title: Method 2 — repeated division by 2 (read remainders bottom-up)

blocks.content: Each hex digit = exactly 4 bits, so split the binary number into **nibbles from the right**.
Write the place values above the bits when converting — it prevents most mistakes and shows your **working**, which earns method marks.

items: **Shorter** and easier for humans to read and write than binary (one hex digit for every 4 bits).
**Fewer errors** when copying long binary values.
Converts to and from binary **very easily** (unlike denary).
Used for: **memory addresses**, **colour codes** in HTML/CSS (`#FF8800`), **MAC addresses** (`3C:52:82:1A:9F:04`), error/debug codes and machine code listings.

blocks.content: Hexadecimal is for **humans** — the computer still stores everything in binary. Hex does **not** use less memory.

**Overflow:** if the result needs more bits than are available (e.g. more than 8 bits for a byte), the extra carry is lost and the stored result is wrong. 11111111 + 00000001 in 8 bits gives 00000000 with a carry out.
Multiply by each bit of the second number (shifted left), then add — exactly like long multiplication in denary, but each partial product is either 0 or the first number.
Multiplying by 2 in binary = **shift left one place** (add a 0 on the right). Multiplying by 4 = shift left two places.

questions.title: Denary to 8-bit binary
questions.text: Convert the denary number **77** to an **8-bit** binary number.

scheme.explanation: 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 77 → 0100 1101. All 8 bits are required, including the leading zero.

content.hint: Convert each group of 4 bits separately.

questions.title: Advantages of hexadecimal
questions.text: Explain **two** advantages of using hexadecimal rather than binary to represent values such as memory addresses.

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 mark per advantage with explanation, max 2:
- Shorter / fewer digits (1 hex digit = 4 bits) so quicker to read/write
- Easier for humans to understand/remember
- Fewer mistakes when reading/copying than long binary strings
- Easy/direct conversion to and from binary (each digit maps to a nibble)

points.criterion: First valid advantage explained (shorter / easier to read / fewer errors / easy conversion)

scheme.model_answer: Hexadecimal is much shorter than binary because each hex digit represents 4 bits, so addresses are quicker to read and write. It is also less error-prone: a programmer is less likely to make a mistake copying '3F2A' than '0011111100101010'.
scheme.ai_instructions: Do not award 'computers use hexadecimal' or 'hexadecimal takes less memory' — both are incorrect (computers store binary). Two points that are the same idea (e.g. 'shorter' and 'fewer digits') earn only 1 mark.

questions.title: Uses of hexadecimal
questions.text: Select **two** places where hexadecimal is commonly used.

options.content: Storing numbers inside the CPU's registers
Counting characters in a text file

scheme.explanation: Registers store binary, not hexadecimal. Hex is a human-readable representation used for colour codes, MAC addresses, memory addresses and error codes.

questions.title: Binary addition and overflow
questions.text:
Add the two 8-bit binary numbers and give the 8-bit result.

```
  0110 1011
+ 0011 0110
```

content.hint: Work from right to left and remember to carry.

scheme.explanation: 107 + 54 = 161 = 1010 0001. The result fits in 8 bits, so there is no overflow.

questions.title: Overflow
questions.text: Adding the 8-bit numbers `1100 0000` and `0100 0001` causes an overflow error.

scheme.explanation: 192 + 65 = 257, which is greater than 255 — the largest value that 8 bits can hold — so a ninth bit is needed.

questions.title: Binary multiplication
questions.text: Multiply the binary numbers `1101` and `101`. Show your working and give the answer in binary.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 mark: correct partial products shown (1101 and 110100). 1 mark: correct answer 1000001 (13 × 5 = 65).

points.criterion: Correct method: partial products / shifting shown

scheme.ai_instructions: The final answer may be written as 1000001 or 0100 0001. Award the method mark for shifted partial products even if the final addition is wrong.
